messages.author: 6b3b475e6af83898
messages.subject: Speeding multilevel IRT
parts:
I have a multi-level IRT model (graded response model for a Likert questionnaire) that seems to be converging quite slowly. The dataset involves ~6000 students in 5 countries, with 42 questions. I’m modeling effects of sex and religion, allowing the effects to vary by country. There are enough moving parts here that it may just be that I have to accept long run times to get convergence, but if anyone has advice on how to speed this up, I’d appreciate it. The model seems to need at least 500 iterations for good convergence, which takes a day or so to run 3 parallel chains on my 4-core 2.8 GHz i7 Macbook. Anything that could cut that time down would be great.

I also wonder whether I’m handling the multi-level modeling of sex and religion right. I feel like I ought to be modeling the group-level variations using a covariance matrix as discussed in section 9.9 of the manual (and Chapter 13 of Gelman and Hill), but I can’t quite figure out how to make that work with categorical variables like sex and religion. Is it necessary (or meaningful) to be working from a covariance matrix for such variables anyway, or is the system I have here OK?

Many thanks,
Josh

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Speeding multilevel IRT
parts:
I'm not sure about the modeling issues, but for efficiency,
you want to take loops like this:

for (i in 1:C) {
gamma_raw_c[i]~normal(gamma_raw,sigma_gamma_c[i]);
beta_c[i]~normal(beta,sigma_beta_c[i]);
}

and vectorize them to:

gamma_raw_c ~ normal(gamma_raw, sigma_gamma_c);
beta_c ~ normal(beta, sigma_beta_c);

It won't be a huge speed improvement because the scales vary.

For an IRT model, this parameterization

for (n in 1:N) {
p[n] <- (gamma_c[cc[jj[n]],kk[n]]) *(alpha[jj[n]]
-beta_c[cc[jj[n]],kk[n]] +delta );
y[n] ~ ordered_logistic(p[n],c[kk[n]]);
}

is confusing me. You use jj for indexes all around. Shouldn't
there be students and questiosn with separate indexing?

The usual IRT model would be:

gamma[j] * (alpha[i] - beta[j])

where gamma is discriminativeness and beta difficulty for problem
j and alpha is ability for student i. An easier-to-sample-from parameterization
is:

(gamma[j] * alpha[i]) - beta2[j]

where you can recover beta = beta2 ./ gamma (elementwise divide).

The usual problems for these models is identifiability.
So you want to make sure the priors are strong enough or
particular items are fixed in value.

- Bob

messages.author: 6b3b475e6af83898
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Speeding multilevel IRT
parts:
Thanks. The use of jj for indexes is because I’m allowing item parameters to vary by country. So gamma_c and beta_c are indexed by country (a property of the individual, hence indexed with jj) and by item (indexed kk).

Identification seems to be working well. I rescale the person parameters by dividing out the sd of the computed values after accounting for the multi-level hierarchy, thus controlling multiplicative nonidentification, and the location priors/hyperpriors on alpha and beta is set to 0, with the offset delta modeled separately. In the reparameterization below, I’d probably keep delta inside the parentheses and let it be mu_alpha, holding mu_beta at 0.

I’ll be interested to test the effects of vectorizing the country-level sampling statements and reparameterizing the IRT model.

I assume there’s no way to effect the Matt trick here?

On Apr 24, 2014, at 6:20 PM, Joshua Rosenau <josh.r...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Thanks. The use of jj for indexes is because I'm allowing item parameters to vary by country. So gamma_c and beta_c are indexed by country (a property of the individual, hence indexed with jj) and by item (indexed kk).
>
> Identification seems to be working well. I rescale the person parameters by dividing out the sd of the computed values after accounting for the multi-level hierarchy, thus controlling multiplicative nonidentification, and the location priors/hyperpriors on alpha and beta is set to 0, with the offset delta modeled separately. In the reparameterization below, I'd probably keep delta inside the parentheses and let it be mu_alpha, holding mu_beta at 0.

Andrew and Jennifer suggest that in their regression book, but we don't recommend
it with HMC. The problem is that the model's still unidentified on the space over
which sampling is happening, which makes it hard for adaptation to find a reasonable
scale.

>
> I'll be interested to test the effects of vectorizing the country-level sampling statements and reparameterizing the IRT model.
>
> I assume there's no way to effect the Matt trick here?

You could do that with the parameters. If you have a lot of data, it's probably
not necessary, but if the data sizes used for estimating any of the coefficients
is small, then going to the uncentered (Matt trick) parameterization would probably
help, too. We haven't experimented with it for IRT specifically (as far as I know), so
I'd be interested in hearing the results.

- Bob
